video.title: Build This Foundation - The Rest Will Follow

classification.reason: The coach provides executable drills and cues including swinging a 2.5-pound weight, using the 'place and pull forward' mental cue, and mini-tennis foundation practice.

problem.title_as_question: How do you build the simplest possible effective forehand foundation?
problem.definition: Developing a minimalist, highly controllable forehand foundation by maintaining posterior shoulder engagement, elbow space, and upper-body synchronization before layering on speed or shape.

symptoms.description: Loss of fault tolerance and diminished ability to move the racket reliably through the desired trajectory in the air.
The racket head whips around early in an excessively wristy motion because the arm is disconnected from the trunk.
Shanking balls and losing control of the racket face angle through impact.

causes.statement: Players relax the muscles behind the arm (lats and posterior shoulder), failing to hold the racket up and disconnecting the arm from the body.
Players actively drop their elbow and racket excessively into the body on higher balls, collapsing elbow space and ruining swing control.
The left side, right side, and trunk become desynchronized and move in conflicting directions instead of moving together as a unified piece.

angles.summary: The posterior shoulder and lat muscles hold the racket up and connect the arm to the trunk, preserving critical elbow space.
Using a 2.5-pound weight stresses the back muscles so the player distinctly feels the muscular activation required to hold the arm up.
Imagining a table at chest height provides a flat guide to slide the racket forward along rather than actively dropping it.
Players often think they must actively drop the racket head to hit low-to-high, which destroys timing, rhythm, and stability.
Demonstrating fully relaxed swings shows that although the motion looks acceptable on camera, it results in an early wristy whip and complete loss of control.

solutions.summary: Perform shadow swings holding a 2.5-pound weight instead of a racket to feel the posterior shoulder and lat muscles engage to support the arm.
solutions.external_goal: hold a 2.5-pound weight up through the swing

solutions.summary: Adopt the mental conception to simply place the hand out and pull the racket forward rather than actively rolling the racket backward.
solutions.external_goal: place the hand out and pull the racket forward

solutions.summary: Imagine a table at chest height, holding the arm up and sliding the racket forward along the table without actively dropping it.
solutions.external_goal: press the racket forward along an imaginary table

solutions.summary: Pair the unit turn with a unit swing so the chest, both arms, and upper body turn back together and come forward together as one piece.
Tilt the hitting shoulder below the non-hitting shoulder to achieve a low-to-high swing path while keeping elbow space and foundation intact.
Warm up by rallying in mini tennis using strictly the simplest effective forehand, holding the racket up with upper back tension through contact.
solutions.external_goal: rally in mini tennis using only the compact contact motion
